content:
<Rep. Mark Takano>: This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to establish two grant programs, which the bill's proponents claim will expand research and improve treatment for mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Committee Democrats and VA have numerous concerns about the bill and, to address these concerns, offered eight amendments at the subcommittee and full committee markups. However, all of these amendments were rejected by the majority.
We strongly oppose this legislation because, if sufficient funds are not appropriated, it would siphon funds away from existing VA mental health treatment and research programs, by requiring VA to use existing funds appropriated for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) research and general mental health services to fund these grant programs. Further, the bill creates an inappropriate structure to administer one of the grant programs, by requiring VA to contract with a third-party entity to perform the inherently governmental responsibilities of allocating and overseeing the expenditure of grant funds. Additionally, the bill does not contain sufficient or robust guardrails to provide oversight of the grantees. Many of these concerns were echoed by VA's testimony at a January 13, 2026, Health Subcommittee legislative hearing where this bill was considered.
In particular, we share VA's concerns that the methodologies and approaches to clinical trials funded by the grant programs established ``would not result in or contribute to actual clinical care; at most, they seem to be a preliminary step toward research that may eventually produce new treatment approaches. This uncertain return on investment of funds VA could otherwise use to provide evidence-based treatments for mTBI is inadvisable. Funds made available for clinical care should be used to deliver clinical care.''
The Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute (A.N.S.) to the bill considered and adopted at the Health Subcommittee markup held on April 16, 2026, made some changes requested by Committee Democrats, but it did not fully address all of our concerns with the bill. Specifically, the A.N.S. changed the grantee eligibility criteria for both grant programs, to require that they have demonstrated some ability to carry out clinical trials, but the amendment did not go far enough to prevent unqualified entities from receiving grants.
The A.N.S. adopted at the Subcommittee markup also included some language requiring grantees to better coordinate care and refer veterans back to VA services, but it didn't address our underlying concern that this legislation will divert care and funding from VA research and mental health services. While it added some new reporting requirements to ensure accountability for grantees, it did not go far enough to ensure that outcomes are properly evaluated or that adverse outcomes are required to be reported in a timely manner.
Finally, the A.N.S. struck language requiring the grant program to ``align'' their activities with the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Grant program. The original language raised serious concerns that the goal of the program was to increase the likelihood of existing Fox Grant grantees receiving these new grants. Committee Democrats appreciate this change, considering it did not make sense for a grant program that is primarily focused on research and clinical treatment to ``align'' with a grant program that is primarily focused on upstream factors of suicide risk, such as financial wellbeing, and not clinical treatment or research.
However, the most concerning provisions-the provisions that allow funds to be diverted from existing appropriated sources at VA in the absence of sufficient funding and the requirement for VA to contract with a third-party entity to administer the grant program in Section 3-were not addressed by the A.N.S. at the Subcommittee markup.
During consideration of the bill at the Health Subcommittee markup, Democratic members offered four amendments, all of which were rejected by Republican members.
Specifically, Representative Morrison offered an amendment that would have strengthened oversight requirements by requiring grantees to collect adverse event data during clinical trials, added requirements to use accepted clinical standards to evaluate the effectiveness of clinical trial outcomes, and expanded the reporting requirements to ensure Congress can perform robust oversight of the programs. The Majority opposed this amendment on grounds that made it clear they are not interested in oversight and would prefer the funding from these grant programs be provided with as few guardrails as possible.
Representative Conaway offered an amendment that would have lowered the maximum grant amount per grantee per fiscal year from $5 million to $2.5 million. The grant program only authorizes $10 million per fiscal year, so if VA awards the maximum amount, only two awards would be given each fiscal year. Given that clinical trial results are not guaranteed to be successful or usable for VA, Committee Democrats believe $5 million is too much funding to provide to any one grantee to be responsible stewards of taxpayer funding. Republicans rejected this amendment.
Representative Brownley offered an amendment that would have stricken provisions within Sec. 2 and Sec. 3 of the A.N.S. that would have directed VA to fund the two grant programs from appropriations for its National Center for PTSD and VA mental health services, if Congress failed to appropriate specific funds for the two grant programs. Because the A.N.S. included the authorization of appropriations, as well as a provision to pay for the legislation using home loan fees, it is very difficult to understand this funding structure--which Committee staff have yet to see in any other bill before now--as anything other than a drain on the resources that VA can use to advance the study and treatment of PTSD and provide direct mental health care to veterans who need it. The Majority rejected this amendment but did not explain how they would ensure that this bill does not divert funding from existing VA appropriations.
Representative Brownley offered another amendment that would have prohibited grantees from receiving grants under both programs during the same fiscal year. The A.N.S. made it possible for certain grantees to be eligible for both grant programs, which could lead to a single grantee receiving up to $6.5 million in a single fiscal year ($5 million under the first grant program and $1.5 million under the second). Republicans also rejected this amendment.
During the bill's consideration at a Full Committee markup on May 14, 2026, Committee Democrats offered further amendments to address their concerns.
Representative Morrison again offered the amendment to strengthen oversight requirements that she offered at the subcommittee markup, which was again rejected.
Representative Brownley again offered the amendment to strike the provisions that would require VA to fund the two grant programs with existing PTSD and general mental health services appropriations if specific funding is not appropriated. Republicans again rejected this amendment and again refused to explain why they refused to include any guardrails in the bill that would prevent diverting VA resources to pay for the grant programs.
Ranking Member Takano offered an amendment that would have required grantees to share with VA all clinical data from the clinical trials funded through the grants under section 2, to ensure coordination of efforts, as well as transparency into the reported outcomes of grantees' research. Any research to improve treatments for mTBI must include coordination with VA, including sharing clinical data that could allow VA's world-class research ecosystem to develop the next great breakthrough. If we are using public funds to conduct research outside VA, we must ensure Congress and VA can evaluate the return on our investment, validate findings, and build on the clinical data created with taxpayer funds. Republicans rejected this amendment as well and defended the interests of the private entities who could receive grant funding from having to provide full transparency to VA or Congress.
Finally, Representative Dexter offered an amendment to strike section 3, to address concerns about the lower standard of research for the second grant program and to remove a requirement that VA enter into an agreement with a third-party entity to administer the grant program. Despite the fact that VA also opposed this grant funding administration structure, Republicans also rejected this amendment.
While we certainly understand and agree with the need for expanding research and improving treatments for mTBI, we are concerned that this legislation will lead to greater fragmentation of research and treatment for veterans. For the reasons cited above, Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 6993.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.
